cls: Topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID, phenylacetic acid derivative)
pharm: The diethylamine salt of diclofenac formulated for cutaneous use; after dermal penetration diclofenac inhibits cyclo-oxygenase (COX-1/COX-2), reducing local prostaglandin synthesis and thereby producing localized analgesic and anti-inflammatory effects with low systemic exposure.
quick: Apply 1.16% gel to affected area 3-4 times daily (2-4 g per site), gently rubbed in
Avoid in third trimester (NSAID class - ductus closure); caution earlier
Topical; do not apply to the breast; limited systemic exposure
Caution with extensive/prolonged use - systemic NSAID effects possible
Caution with extensive use; systemic absorption is low topically
Local skin reaction; with large-area/long-term use consider systemic NSAID effects
summary: Diclofenac diethylamine is the diethylammonium salt of the NSAID diclofenac, formulated as a topical gel/emulgel (commonly 1.16%, equivalent to 1% diclofenac sodium) for the local relief of pain and inflammation in soft-tissue and joint conditions - muscle and joint sprains, strains, contusions, tendinitis, and localized osteoarthritis pain. Diclofenac inhibits cyclo-oxygenase and reduces prostaglandin production at the site of application, giving local analgesia with much lower systemic exposure than oral diclofenac. Because it is an NSAID, the labeled cautions of the class still apply with extensive or prolonged use, and it shares NSAID contraindications such as aspirin/NSAID-induced asthma. It should be applied to intact skin only, not to wounds, mucous membranes, or the eyes, and sun exposure of treated skin should be limited (photosensitivity).
indications: Local symptomatic relief of pain and inflammation in trauma of tendons, ligaments, muscles and joints (e.g. sprains, strains, contusions)
Localized forms of soft-tissue rheumatism (e.g. tendinitis, bursitis, periarthritis)
Localized pain relief in osteoarthritis of superficial joints such as the knees and hands

dosage.d: Apply 2-4 g (an amount the size of a cherry to a walnut) to the affected area 3-4 times daily and rub in gently
dosage.n: Daily dose generally should not exceed about 16 g per joint for lower limbs / 8 g for upper limbs in OA use

dosage.d: Apply to the painful area 3-4 times daily for the duration of symptoms (typically up to 7-14 days for acute injury without medical review)
dosage.n: Reassess if no improvement within 7 days (self-treatment)

dosage.d: Use in children/adolescents only as directed by a physician per product labeling

admin: Apply only to intact, healthy skin over the painful area and rub in gently
Wash hands after application (unless the hands are being treated)
Do not apply to broken skin, wounds, mucous membranes, or the eyes
Do not cover treated skin with an occlusive/airtight dressing
Avoid excessive sun or UV exposure of treated areas (risk of photosensitivity)
Do not use with other topical or oral NSAIDs on the same area without medical advice
moa: Diclofenac is a phenylacetic acid NSAID that inhibits the cyclo-oxygenase enzymes (COX-1 and COX-2), blocking the conversion of arachidonic acid to prostaglandins that mediate pain, inflammation, and swelling. Applied topically as the diethylamine salt, it penetrates the skin to reach underlying inflamed tissue, where local inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis produces analgesic and anti-inflammatory effects. Because absorption into the systemic circulation is low relative to oral dosing, therapeutic concentrations are concentrated at the application site, limiting systemic effects when used as directed.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to diclofenac or any excipient
Patients in whom aspirin or other NSAIDs precipitate asthma, urticaria, or acute rhinitis (NSAID/aspirin-sensitive)
Application to damaged/non-intact skin, open wounds, infected/eczematous skin, mucous membranes or the eyes
relative: Extensive or prolonged use (systemic NSAID risks - GI, renal, cardiovascular)
History of NSAID-related GI bleeding or peptic ulcer
Renal or hepatic impairment with extensive use
monitor: Systemic NSAID adverse effects if applied to large areas for prolonged periods

preg: Use should be avoided in the third trimester of pregnancy because NSAIDs (including diclofenac) can cause premature closure of the fetal ductus arteriosus, oligohydramnios, and inhibition of labor. In the first and second trimesters topical diclofenac should be used only if clearly necessary and at the lowest effective amount. Systemic exposure from topical use is low but the NSAID class precautions apply.
lact: Systemic absorption from topical use is low. Diclofenac passes into breast milk in small amounts after systemic use. While breastfeeding, do not apply to the breast/nipple area, and avoid prolonged use over large skin areas.
renal: Systemic exposure is low with appropriate topical use, so renal effects are unlikely; however, NSAID-related renal risk can occur with extensive or prolonged application or in patients with pre-existing renal impairment, volume depletion, or heart failure - use caution.
hepatic: Topical systemic absorption is low. Use caution with extensive use in patients with hepatic impairment, consistent with NSAID class precautions.

moderate: Oral NSAIDs / aspirin - additive systemic NSAID exposure and adverse effects if used together
Anticoagulants, antiplatelet agents - theoretical increased bleeding risk if substantial systemic absorption occurs
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction with topical use.
interactions.diagnostics: No significant laboratory interference with appropriate topical use.

common: Burning or stinging at the site
serious: Severe allergic/hypersensitivity reaction (including in aspirin/NSAID-sensitive patients - bronchospasm, angioedema)
Systemic NSAID effects (GI, renal, cardiovascular) with extensive/prolonged use
rare: Systemic NSAID reactions when absorbed in significant amounts
emergency: Anaphylaxis or severe bronchospasm in NSAID-sensitive individuals
Signs of GI bleeding or renal impairment with heavy/prolonged use

monitoring: Local skin response at the application site
Photosensitivity if treated skin is sun-exposed
Resolution of symptoms (reassess if no improvement within 7 days of self-treatment)
With extensive/prolonged use, monitor for systemic NSAID effects (GI, renal, cardiovascular)
counsel: Apply only to unbroken skin over the sore area and rub it in gently; wash your hands afterward
Do not use on wounds, broken skin, the eyes, or mouth, and do not cover with an airtight dressing
Keep treated skin out of strong sunlight or sunlamps - it can become more sensitive
If you are sensitive to aspirin or other anti-inflammatory drugs (e.g. they cause wheezing or rash), tell your doctor before using
Avoid the last 3 months of pregnancy and check with your doctor before use if pregnant
Stop and see a doctor if the skin reacts badly or if your pain does not improve within about 7 days
pk: Local analgesic effect develops over hours of regular application
Low systemic plasma levels; local tissue concentrations build with repeated use
Systemic diclofenac half-life ~1-2 hours (low systemic exposure topically)
Dosed 3-4 times daily to maintain local effect
Store at room temperature; keep the tube closed and away from heat/flame (flammable gel base)
pearls: Diclofenac topical gels are FDA-approved (diclofenac sodium 1%); the diethylamine salt (1.16% emulgel, e.g. Voltaren Emulgel) is widely marketed in the EU/India - faithful info here is from the EU SmPC/BNF for the diethylamine salt
Topical NSAID gives local analgesia with much lower systemic exposure than oral diclofenac - useful where systemic NSAID risk is a concern
Still carries NSAID class cautions - avoid in aspirin/NSAID-induced asthma and the third trimester of pregnancy
Apply to intact skin only; avoid occlusive dressings and limit sun exposure (photosensitivity)
Reassess self-treatment if no benefit within ~7 days
Extensive or prolonged application can produce systemic NSAID effects - keep within labeled amounts
missed: This medicine is applied as needed for pain, so there is no strict dosing schedule to miss. If you forget an application, apply it when you remember, then continue your usual routine without applying extra. Do not exceed the maximum number of applications per day.
overdose: Overdose is unlikely with topical use because of low systemic absorption. Excessive application over large areas could lead to systemic NSAID effects. Accidental ingestion of the gel could cause systemic NSAID toxicity (GI upset, in large amounts CNS and renal effects). Management is supportive and symptomatic; remove excess gel from the skin and seek medical advice after significant ingestion.
